lesson_title: Select Missing Word and Highlight Incorrect Words

overview.what_it_is: This lesson teaches two PTE Academic listening item types. Select Missing Word requires the test taker to predict how a short recording ends by combining topic, vocabulary, grammar, and discourse clues. Highlight Incorrect Words requires the test taker to follow a written transcript while listening and select only the words that differ from the recording. Together, the tasks develop predictive listening, accurate speech-to-text matching, vocabulary awareness, grammatical anticipation, concentration, and sentence-stress recognition.

format_facts.label: Select Missing Word input
format_facts.value: You listen to a recording that usually lasts about 20–70 seconds, with the final word or short ending replaced by a sound.

format_facts.label: Select Missing Word response
format_facts.value: You choose one answer from several options to complete the speaker's final idea.

format_facts.label: Select Missing Word scoring
format_facts.value: The response is scored as correct or incorrect, so one final selection must be made.

format_facts.label: Highlight Incorrect Words input
format_facts.value: You read a transcript on screen while listening to the corresponding recording.

format_facts.label: Highlight Incorrect Words response
format_facts.value: You click the written words that do not match what the speaker actually says.

format_facts.label: Listening condition
format_facts.value: The recording should be treated as a one-listen task, so preparation, continuous tracking, and immediate decisions are essential.

scoring_factors.name: Select Missing Word — correct/incorrect
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Scored correct or incorrect only: 1 point for the correct option, 0 for an incorrect one. The official Score Guide lists no separate scoring traits for this item type.

scoring_factors.name: Highlight Incorrect Words — partial credit
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Scored per word with partial credit: you gain credit for each correctly identified word, and points are deducted for words you select incorrectly. The official Score Guide lists no separate scoring traits for this item type.

critical_rules: In Select Missing Word, listen for the speaker's overall conclusion rather than relying only on the final few words.
Use the answer options after understanding the recording; do not choose an option only because it sounds familiar.
If uncertain in Select Missing Word, make the best evidence-based guess because leaving the item unanswered cannot earn credit.
In Highlight Incorrect Words, skim the transcript before the recording starts so you know the topic and sentence structure.
Keep following the transcript even after detecting a mismatch; do not stop mentally to analyse one word.
Click a word in Highlight Incorrect Words only when you are confident that the spoken word is different.
Treat different pronunciation, accent, or reduced speech as a possible listening difficulty, not automatically as a transcript error.
Pay special attention to stressed content words, contrasts, negatives, numbers, prefixes, and suffixes.

learning_goals: Identify the topic, theme, and likely direction of a short academic recording.
Use topic knowledge to predict how a speaker may complete an idea.
Use vocabulary collocations to identify natural and unnatural answer choices.
Use grammar to determine the required part of speech, tense, number, or phrase structure.
Recognize conclusion signals and predict the speaker's final message.
Track a written transcript continuously while listening to natural speech.
Distinguish genuine word substitutions from accent, linking, reduction, and pronunciation variation.
Use sentence stress to focus attention on important information words.
Apply different guessing rules to the two item types.
Complete both tasks accurately under realistic one-listen conditions.

core_method.name: Predict, Track, Verify
core_method.summary: For Select Missing Word, build a prediction from the whole recording and verify it against the options. For Highlight Incorrect Words, preview the transcript, track the speaker word by word, and select only confirmed mismatches while continuing to follow the text.

steps.detail: Quickly inspect the prompt, transcript, or answer choices. Identify the likely topic and notice important nouns, verbs, linkers, negatives, and sentence endings.
For Select Missing Word, listen for the speaker's conclusion. For Highlight Incorrect Words, prepare to compare sound and text continuously.
Identify what the speaker is discussing, whether the attitude is positive, negative, uncertain, or contrasting, and where the argument is moving.
Listen for linkers such as however, therefore, in conclusion, despite this, and as a result because they reveal the relationship between ideas.
Use collocation and grammar to predict the kind of word or phrase that should appear next, including its part of speech and meaning.
During Highlight Incorrect Words, move through the transcript at the speaker's pace and resist looking back at earlier lines.
Compare the predicted meaning with the Select Missing Word options, or compare the exact spoken word with the transcript before clicking.
Choose the strongest supported option in Select Missing Word, but remain conservative and click only confirmed differences in Highlight Incorrect Words.

core_method.formula: Select Missing Word: Topic + Discourse direction + Collocation + Grammar = Best ending. Highlight Incorrect Words: Preview + Track + Hear exact word + Confirm difference = Click.

techniques.name: Three-Clue Prediction
techniques.purpose: To predict a missing word or ending by combining several independent clues instead of relying on intuition alone.
how_to: Identify the topic of the recording or sentence.
Check which words commonly appear together as a collocation.
Determine the grammatical form required in the gap.
Choose the option that satisfies meaning, vocabulary, and grammar at the same time.
techniques.example: In 'Can you guess the missing ___?', the topic is a gap activity, 'missing word' is a common collocation, and a noun is required after the adjective 'missing'.
techniques.why_it_matters: An option supported by several clues is more reliable than one selected because of a single familiar word.
techniques.common_error: Choosing an option that matches the topic but does not fit the grammar or collocation.

techniques.name: Conclusion-Signal Listening
techniques.purpose: To recognize when the speaker is presenting the final point that the missing ending must complete.
how_to: Listen for signals such as therefore, so, overall, in conclusion, and this means.
Notice whether the speaker is summarizing, warning, recommending, or rejecting an idea.
Reduce the recording to a short final message in your own words.
Match that message to the option with the same logical meaning.
techniques.example: If a speaker describes repeated claims but says there is no reliable evidence, the final answer should express doubt rather than certainty.
techniques.why_it_matters: Select Missing Word usually depends on the direction of the whole recording, especially its final conclusion.
techniques.common_error: Selecting an answer based on one detail from the middle of the recording instead of the final argument.

techniques.name: Grammar-Slot Analysis
techniques.purpose: To eliminate answer choices that cannot fit the missing grammatical position.
how_to: Listen to the words immediately before the missing section.
Decide whether the gap needs a noun, verb, adjective, adverb, clause, or fixed phrase.
Check agreement, tense, singular or plural form, and required prepositions.
Remove options that create an incomplete or ungrammatical sentence.
techniques.example: After 'The research was not sufficiently...', an adjective such as 'reliable' is more likely than a noun such as 'reliability'.
techniques.why_it_matters: Grammar can eliminate attractive distractors before meaning is considered in detail.
techniques.common_error: Ignoring word form because two answer choices have similar meanings.

techniques.name: Eyes-Forward Tracking
techniques.purpose: To maintain the speaker's position in the transcript during Highlight Incorrect Words.
how_to: Skim the transcript before listening and note sentence boundaries.
Follow the text with your eyes at the speaker's pace.
When a mismatch occurs, select it quickly and continue moving forward.
Use punctuation and line breaks to recover your place if you temporarily lose synchronization.
techniques.example: If the recording says 'friends' while the transcript shows 'colleagues', select 'colleagues' and immediately continue to the next words.
techniques.why_it_matters: Stopping to analyse one mismatch can cause several later differences to be missed.
techniques.common_error: Looking back repeatedly at an earlier word and losing the current position.

techniques.name: Stress-Target Checking
techniques.purpose: To use sentence stress as an attention guide for important or contrasting information.
how_to: Expect nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs, numbers, and negatives to receive stronger stress.
Check stressed words carefully against the transcript.
Listen for stressed prefixes or suffixes that create contrast, such as legal versus illegal.
Continue checking unstressed words, but give priority to information-bearing words.
techniques.example: In 'The policy was INeffective, not effective', stress highlights the prefix that changes the meaning.
techniques.why_it_matters: Many meaningful substitutions occur in content words, and speakers often emphasize contrasts that reveal them.
techniques.common_error: Assuming every stressed word must be incorrect or ignoring small but meaningful affixes.

techniques.name: Sound-versus-Word Verification
techniques.purpose: To avoid selecting a correct transcript word simply because natural pronunciation makes it sound unfamiliar.
how_to: Consider linking, weak forms, contractions, and reduced sounds before deciding a word is different.
Ask whether the sound could be a normal pronunciation of the written word.
Check the surrounding grammar and meaning.
Select the transcript word only when a different lexical word was actually spoken.
techniques.example: The phrase 'going to' may sound like 'gonna' in natural speech, but this pronunciation difference does not necessarily mean the transcript is incorrect.
techniques.why_it_matters: Highlight Incorrect Words tests word differences, not minor accent or pronunciation variation.
techniques.common_error: Clicking a correctly transcribed word because the speaker reduced or linked its sounds.

worked_examples.title: Predicting a Missing Noun
worked_examples.input: Sentence ending: 'Can you guess the missing ___?' Options: message, word, silently, complete.
worked_examples.decoding: The activity concerns guessing something absent from a sentence. The adjective 'missing' normally modifies a noun, and 'missing word' is a common collocation.
worked_examples.plan: Check the topic, identify the required part of speech, test each option as a natural collocation, and select the only option supported by all three clues.

annotations.comment: The sentence describes a language-gap activity.
'Missing word' is a frequent and natural collocation.
A noun is required after the adjective 'missing'.
'Silently' is an adverb, 'complete' does not fit naturally, and 'message' is less contextually precise.

worked_examples.title: Selecting the Speaker's Final Conclusion
worked_examples.input: Recording summary: A speaker describes a famous lost-island story, explains that many people believe it, but repeatedly notes that no reliable physical evidence has been found. Options include certainty that the island existed, doubt about the story, a travel recommendation, and a description of modern islands.
worked_examples.decoding: The main contrast is between a popular belief and the absence of proof. The ending must reflect the speaker's conclusion, not an interesting supporting detail.
worked_examples.plan: Identify the topic, mark the contrast signalled by 'but', paraphrase the final attitude as 'the claim remains unproven', and select the option expressing doubt.
worked_examples.model_answer: Choose the option stating that the story cannot be accepted as fact because convincing evidence is missing.

annotations.comment: The recording concerns a legendary island.
Popular belief is contrasted with a lack of evidence.
The speaker is cautious and unconvinced.
An option mentioning islands may share vocabulary but fail to express the conclusion.

worked_examples.title: Confirming a Spoken-Transcript Substitution
worked_examples.input: Transcript: 'The researchers discussed the result with their colleagues before publishing the report.' Recording: 'The researchers discussed the result with their friends before publishing the report.'
worked_examples.decoding: Every part matches except the noun after 'their'. The recording contains 'friends', while the written transcript contains 'colleagues'.
worked_examples.plan: Track continuously, compare the exact noun heard with the noun displayed, select the written mismatch, and continue following the sentence.

annotations.comment: The spoken and written nouns are different lexical items.
Select the incorrect written word, not the word that was spoken.
Both nouns fit grammatically, so meaning and sound comparison are required.
The learner should click quickly and continue rather than replaying the difference mentally.

worked_examples.title: Using Stress to Detect a Meaning Change
worked_examples.input: Transcript: 'The new treatment was effective in every trial.' Recording: 'The new treatment was ineffective in every trial.'
worked_examples.decoding: The speaker stresses the negative prefix in 'ineffective'. The transcript omits that prefix and therefore states the opposite meaning.
worked_examples.plan: Notice the stressed contrast, verify the whole spoken word, compare it with the transcript, and select the incorrect written form.

annotations.comment: The prefix 'in-' may receive emphasis because it reverses the meaning.
The transcript word 'effective' is the item to select.
The selection is justified by an exact lexical difference, not merely by pronunciation.

items.when_to_use: Expect a result, consequence, or logical conclusion to follow.
Prepare for the speaker's final summary or judgement.
Listen for a general evaluation that combines earlier points.
Expect the speaker to explain the implication of the previous information.
Expect the speaker to change direction or introduce an opposing point.
Listen for a contrast between two connected facts.
Expect a preference or correction between alternatives.
Prepare for clarification, stronger evidence, or correction of an earlier assumption.
Expect a reason or explanation.
Expect a consequence that may help predict the final idea.
Listen for the cause of a situation or conclusion.
Expect the speaker to state the logical outcome of earlier information.

items.item: This option matches the speaker's conclusion.
items.when_to_use: Use during review to justify the final Select Missing Word choice.

items.item: This option fits the topic but not the grammar.
items.when_to_use: Use when eliminating a semantically related but grammatically impossible distractor.

items.item: This option repeats a detail, not the main point.
items.when_to_use: Use when an answer is based on supporting information rather than the speaker's final message.

items.item: This option creates a natural collocation.
items.when_to_use: Use when vocabulary partnership supports one answer more strongly than the others.
Use only after confirming an exact spoken-transcript substitution.

items.item: The pronunciation changed, but the word is the same.
items.when_to_use: Use to avoid false selections caused by accent, linking, or reduction.
Use when comparing forms such as possible and impossible.

items.item: I am not certain, so I will not click.
items.when_to_use: Use as the decision rule for uncertain Highlight Incorrect Words selections.

common_mistakes.mistake: Trying to predict the Select Missing Word answer from the options before understanding the recording.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The options can create false expectations and distract attention from the speaker's actual argument.
common_mistakes.fix: First identify the topic and conclusion, then evaluate the options against your prediction.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using only topic similarity to choose an answer.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Several distractors may contain words connected to the topic but fail to complete the grammar or logic.
common_mistakes.fix: Require support from topic, collocation, grammar, and discourse direction.

common_mistakes.mistake: Refusing to guess in Select Missing Word when uncertain.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: An unanswered item cannot be correct, while an evidence-based guess still has a chance of earning credit.
common_mistakes.fix: Eliminate weak options and select the strongest remaining answer.

common_mistakes.mistake: Guess-clicking uncertain words in Highlight Incorrect Words.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Incorrect selections can reduce the benefit of correct identifications.
common_mistakes.fix: Click only when a different spoken word has been clearly confirmed.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stopping after finding one incorrect word.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The recording continues, and later mismatches may be missed.
common_mistakes.fix: Select quickly and keep moving forward with the speaker.

common_mistakes.mistake: Looking back at earlier lines of the transcript.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Backward eye movement causes the listener to lose synchronization with the audio.
common_mistakes.fix: Use an eyes-forward rule and recover at the next punctuation mark if needed.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating accent or reduced pronunciation as a word substitution.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The transcript may be correct even when the word sounds unfamiliar in connected speech.
common_mistakes.fix: Check whether linking, contractions, weak forms, or accent can explain the sound.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Although content words are often stressed, errors may also occur in articles, auxiliaries, prepositions, or negatives.
common_mistakes.fix: Use stress to guide attention, but continue comparing the complete transcript.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reading a practice transcript unnaturally slowly.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Slow word-by-word reading does not prepare learners for natural test speed, stress, or connected speech.
common_mistakes.fix: Read clearly at a natural rate, pause according to punctuation, and continue through the whole passage.

time_budget.focus: Review the two formats, scoring logic, and the opposite guessing rules.
Practise topic, vocabulary, collocation, and grammar clues.
Listen for discourse direction, conclusions, and final-answer meaning.
Skim passages, follow punctuation, and maintain eyes-forward synchronization.
Compare stressed content words, prefixes, suffixes, negatives, and similar-sounding words.
Complete both item types under one-listen test conditions.
Classify errors as topic, vocabulary, grammar, tracking, sound discrimination, or over-clicking problems.

drills.name: Three-Clue Gap Drill
drills.instructions: Complete short sentence gaps and write one topic clue, one collocation clue, and one grammar clue for every answer.

drills.name: Part-of-Speech Elimination
drills.instructions: Use answer sets containing nouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; identify the required form before considering meaning.

drills.name: Final-Idea Paraphrase
drills.instructions: Listen to a short recording, pause before the ending, and state the expected conclusion in five to eight words before viewing the options.

drills.name: Linker Prediction
drills.instructions: After hearing however, therefore, although, or as a result, predict whether the next idea will contrast, conclude, concede, or show a consequence.

drills.name: Moving-Finger Tracking
drills.instructions: Follow a printed transcript with a finger or cursor while a partner reads it naturally, keeping movement continuous and forward.

drills.name: Controlled Substitution Reading
drills.instructions: A partner reads a transcript but secretly replaces four words; underline only the confirmed written mismatches.

drills.name: Stress Contrast Drill
drills.instructions: Practise pairs such as possible/impossible, effective/ineffective, legal/illegal, and increase/decrease, emphasizing the contrasting sound.

drills.name: One-Listen Confidence Review
drills.instructions: After each Highlight Incorrect Words item, label every click as certain, probable, or guessed, then remove guessed selections from future attempts.

practice_plan.routine: Use a four-round routine. Round 1: complete prediction exercises without audio. Round 2: listen to short endings and explain the topic, collocation, and grammar evidence. Round 3: compare audio with transcripts while maintaining forward tracking. Round 4: complete a timed mixed set, review every wrong answer, and record the cause of the error in a study log.

mastery_checklist: I can explain the difference between Select Missing Word and Highlight Incorrect Words.
I can identify the topic of a short recording before it ends.
I can recognize linkers that signal contrast, cause, result, and conclusion.
I can use collocations to predict natural missing language.
I can determine the grammatical form required by a missing section.
I can choose an answer that matches the speaker's final idea rather than a minor detail.
I can skim a transcript efficiently before listening begins.
I can follow a transcript continuously without repeatedly looking back.
I can identify exact spoken-transcript substitutions.
I can distinguish pronunciation variation from a genuine word difference.
I can use sentence stress to prioritize important information words.
I can continue tracking after selecting an incorrect written word.
I can make an evidence-based guess in Select Missing Word.
I can avoid uncertain clicks in Highlight Incorrect Words.
I can complete both item types under realistic one-listen conditions.
strategy_notes: The two tasks require different risk strategies: make a best guess in Select Missing Word, but avoid guessing in Highlight Incorrect Words.
A correct Select Missing Word option should complete both the sentence and the speaker's broader argument.
Predict meaning before inspecting the options too closely, because options can contain misleading topic vocabulary.
The final missing section may depend on information introduced much earlier in the recording.
Grammar is especially useful when two options appear to have similar meanings.
During Highlight Incorrect Words, the click target is the incorrect word shown in the transcript.
Natural speech may contain linking, reductions, hesitations, false starts, or accent variation; these do not automatically indicate transcript errors.
Stressed words deserve attention because they commonly carry new, important, negative, numerical, or contrasting information.
Punctuation provides recovery points if tracking is briefly lost.
Do not allow one difficult word to interrupt comprehension of the rest of the recording.
Practising by reading transcripts aloud at natural speed develops awareness of stress, intonation, punctuation, and connected speech.
Error review should identify the failed process, not only the correct answer.
A useful error log can classify mistakes as topic, conclusion, vocabulary, grammar, tracking, pronunciation, or over-selection errors.

metadata.estimated_study_time: Plan for about 2 hours of focused study.
metadata.provenance_note: Teaching-first enrichment based on the supplied Chapter 5 lesson material covering Select Missing Word and Highlight Incorrect Words, including source objectives, format details, prediction strategies, sentence-stress practice, transcript comparison, worked examples, misconceptions, practice questions, and self-check outcomes. Correction: an earlier version of this lesson named four scoring traits ("Final-answer accuracy", "Contextual prediction", "Mismatch identification", "Selection control") that do not exist. The official Score Guide (p.44) lists "Not applicable" for traits on both item types; they are scored correct/incorrect and per-word partial credit respectively. Fixed by the enrichment fact audit.
